item.title: Starlink Speed Test
item.content:encoded:
Download speed is usually what providers and experts refer to when they talk about "internet speed." It measures how your connection performs when data travels from the web server to your device. It determines how fast web pages and files load. You'll want fast download speeds to watch Netflix in 4K.

Upload speed is how quickly data travels from your device to the web server. Upload examples include sharing photos and videos to social media, backing up files to cloud storage, sending emails, and other outgoing tasks. Upload speed can also impact video calls, such as Zoom and FaceTime.

Latency measures how long it takes data to travel from your device to the server and back. It's measured in milliseconds, and the lower the better. One of the biggest contributors to high latency is distance—latency increases the farther you are from the tower or web server you're connected to. It matters most in online gaming, where quick response times are needed.

item.title: Satellite Phone vs. Direct-to-Cell Smartphone: Which Do You Need Off the Grid? (2026)
item.content:encoded:
D2D capability is an up-and-coming feature and is steadily becoming a mainstay for all major mobile carriers. New phone models are being optimized for connecting to satellite networks and related spectrums, so manufacturers and carriers can claim to offer absolute coverage, no matter where you are. However, it still has a long way to go. 

Next to full 5G performance, it's like comparing dial-up to fiber. Most available D2D features are limited to two-way text messaging and emergency SOS, and they're prone to working slowly. Like most satellite technology, it requires a clear view of the sky, and heavy weather can affect the signal. Voice and data are being introduced, but networks still have growing to do to support seamless switching between 5G and satellite.

For deep backcountry travel, oceans, and globetrotting the most remote corners of the world, dedicated satellite phones remain a go-to for experienced explorers who know reliability matters most. 

"While emerging direct-to-device technologies and portable solutions like the Starlink Mini offer convenience and lower costs for casual users, dedicated satellite phones remain essential for mission-critical reliability," said communication and technology executive advisor Jason Todd.

For true global coverage with real-time voice and emergency monitoring, dedicated devices are built for those who need a guaranteed lifeline. They're designed for safety first, with rugged outer cases and lasting battery power. The biggest trade-off is their notoriously high upfront cost and subscription fees.

For now, each technology serves a specific use case. Smartphones for D2D are for rural residents with spotty home coverage, road trippers, day hikers, and casual campers. Dedicated devices are for those with critical needs in the most remote locations where terrestrial connectivity is impossible. Sailors, multi-day backpackers, field workers, and emergency response workers make the most use of dedicated satellite communication devices.

"For high-stakes situations where communication failure is not an option, standalone satellite devices provide dedicated connectivity independent of terrestrial cellular infrastructure," Todd advised. "However, for general off-grid travel, lightweight satellite internet terminals are increasingly becoming the practical choice over traditional hardware."

For the ultimate protection, carrying both is a smart move. Most experts agree this layered approach gives you options, since redundancy across different tech types prepares you for the worst. 

Despite a clear difference between satellite phones and smartphones with satellite features, D2D and LEO satellite technology is still young and continually growing. LEO performance and capacity depend on constellation size, and as multiple providers expand with weekly launches, coverage and capacity could reach a point where worldwide phone signal is ubiquitous.

item.title: Best RV Internet Options (2026): Starlink, T-Mobile, & TravlFi Compared
item.content:encoded:
Once you've chosen your preferred RV internet provider, it's time to get it ready for your trip. Luckily, both of our preferred solutions are incredibly easy to set up in your vehicle. 

Starlink RV setup

When using Starlink on the road, there's a bit of DIY and some extra hardware, but it's still simple.  

Starlink sells vehicle-mounting kits for all its dish models, with a detachable option for roof racks or a permanent mount. The official kits come with step-by-step installation guides for mounting, with a list of tools you'll need. 

There are also third-party mounting kits available online, including less invasive options like suction cup mounts that attach to sunroofs. The Starlink Mini is much easier to set up, and sometimes only needs to be secured to your dashboard.

Powering the Starlink Mini

The Starlink Mini is incredibly power-efficient. While standard Starlink LEO dishes draw 75 to 100 watts of continuous power, the Mini operates at a mere 20 to 40 watts and drops to about 15 watts when idle. This makes it a game-changer for off-grid power management.

  • Standard Power: The base kit includes a standard AC power supply and a heavy 50-foot direct current cable.

  • 12V Vehicle Adaptor: If you want to work from your dashboard or power the dish directly from your RV’s 12V or 24V socket, Starlink sells an official Mini Car Adaptor for $45, which includes the necessary USB-C cable.

  • Power Banks and Third-Party Batteries: The Starlink Mini requires a 100W power source functioning precisely at 20V and 5A. High-capacity laptop power banks work perfectly for this. Alternatively, third-party battery bases that clip directly onto the back of the dish are now available for an all-in-one cord-free setup.

  • The Cable Catch: If you’re opting for a USB-C setup, use Starlink’s official 16-foot USB-C cable. Generic third-party cables often fail to deliver the very specific power profile required to maintain the satellite connection.

T-Mobile AWAY RV setup

The T-Mobile AWAY Gateway device is even easier to set up in your vehicle. Since it uses a 5G signal, which isn't as affected by obstructions as a satellite signal, it doesn't need to be installed outside the vehicle. It just needs to be secured somewhere in your RV, preferably near a window, to get the best signal.

Powering T-Mobile AWAY in Your RV

The T-Mobile AWAY 5G Gateway is primarily designed to run on standard 100–240V household electricity. While this is easy if your rig is plugged in at an RV park, you'll need to get a little creative if you're traveling off the grid:

  • DC Power Inverters: If you want to run the gateway while driving or off your RV’s 12-volt battery bank, you will need a DC power inverter. A basic 100-watt inverter plugged into a 12V auxiliary socket (cigarette lighter) is more than enough to keep the gateway running smoothly.

  • Portable Power Banks: For maximum portability, the T-Mobile AWAY gateway can be powered by a portable power bank connected via a USB-C cable. You need a battery rated for at least 100 watts (the kind used to charge laptops, like the Anker 737). The gateway is relatively power-efficient; running it off a 100W bank for 30 minutes typically drains less than 10% of the battery.

item.title: Best Satellite Phones for Hiking and Off-Grid Travel (2026)
item.content:encoded:
If you’re going on an outdoor expedition or visiting remote areas where cell coverage is limited or non-existent, you might need a satellite phone. But do you know how to find the best satellite phones for your needs? Some satellite phones have a wide range of features and heavy-duty hardware, but not everyone needs a full-featured military-grade satellite phone. For many hikers, climbers, and explorers, a simpler satellite communicator device will be the best choice.

Some satellite communicators can connect to your cell phone to enable satellite coverage, effectively turning your cell phone into a satellite phone. If you want satellite connectivity at a lower cost, satellite communicators offer convenience, lifesaving emergency connectivity, and affordable pricing.

item.title: Is Starlink Worth It in the City? Urban & Suburban Guide
item.content:encoded:
Starlink satellite internet has been promoted primarily as a home internet solution for rural, remote, and off-the-grid locations, but as it has gained popularity since its launch, you may wonder whether it's a viable option for home internet in more populated areas. Starlink can provide internet almost anywhere, so it will work in urban, suburban, and metropolitan areas. However, are the performance, pricing, and setup worth it compared with more traditional providers in the city?

Is Starlink Worth It in the City? Urban & Suburban Guide

Starlink performance and network congestion

In its early days, not everyone could get Starlink, so many were added to a waitlist as the company built out its satellite constellation. Bandwidth can only be spread across so many customers. As of 2026, with more than 10,000 active satellites and more launching all the time, it's large enough to serve millions of customers and reduce network congestion. However, it's hard to determine if it's ready to be a serious competitor to traditional ISPs, including cable, DSL, and fiber. As Starlink is also entering the mobile carrier space with Starlink Mobile, its ambitions likely include general-purpose broadband.

There are more than 10,000 Starlink LEO satellites in orbit. SpaceX is consistantly launching new Starlink satellites to improve signal coverage and relieve network congestion. | Screenshot from satellitemap.space

At any given location, rural or metropolitan, Starlink's performance will vary. Anytime you begin using a Starlink dish, you're instantly competing with fellow customers around you for the satellite constellation's attention. Starlink tries to balance bandwidth between customers in several ways, mostly by expanding the constellation with layers of more advanced satellites that provide more coverage for more users. However, it also regulates congestion by adding one-time "demand surcharges" to regions with heavy usage. These congestion fees can range from $100 to $1,500. It can also limit the plans available to you, restricting access to higher-priority plans like Residential MAX. 

Network congestion exists in both rural and metro areas. It all depends on how many other Starlinks are surrounding you. In fact, because cities typically offer more options, satellite internet congestion is less likely. If there's no demand surcharge and you have access to the full range of plans, you're in the clear to use Starlink in the city.

Setup challenges in the concrete jungle

Even without network congestion, practical challenges remain when running Starlink in a metropolitan area, especially in big cities. The biggest obstacle is obtaining a clear field of view for the Starlink dish. For peak performance, aim for an unobstructed 100-degree view of the sky. Obstructions like neighboring high-rise buildings in the city or dense suburban tree lines can degrade or flat-out block the satellite signal. This can make installation tricky, especially for apartment renters who don't have access or permission to install on the roof. If that's the case, a balcony may be your best option, but if your view is of another skyscraper, you may be out of luck. 

Permanent home installation requires extra equipment and drilling. | Image by Starlink

If you own a home in the suburbs, you'll get the best performance by installing Starlink on the roof. This will require some DIY skills and extra parts, although Starlink offers professional installation (free for MAX customers and at least $199 for other plans).

To ensure Starlink will work at your location, download the Starlink app and use the obstruction tool. Use it to scan the area where you want to install the dish to confirm you have enough clearance to set it up. You don't have to be a Starlink customer to use the app.

A question of cost-effectiveness

So you can get Starlink working in your urban or suburban home without congestion or obstructions, but is it worth it? When you compare the value of satellite vs. wired connections like DSL, cable, or fiber, it's clear which is more affordable. The cost of infrastructure for satellite internet (building up the fleet through launches) accounts for its high monthly pricing. Traditional internet offered in metropolitan areas uses existing infrastructure, or investments from providers or governments, which is the case for fiber, while offering more affordable pricing.

Starlink is also unique in that it sells its equipment at a high upfront cost, with some exceptions in areas where you can rent the dish. Cable and fiber providers usually include equipment leasing in the monthly service charge.

Can Starlink compete with fiber?

While Starlink offers high speeds and low latency, is easy to obtain and install, and can be more affordable in some cases, it still falls short of the many benefits of a fiber connection. Because fiber requires new infrastructure and investment, it has been slower to adopt, but it's still growing in many metropolitan areas. A modest fiber plan can deliver at least 1 Gbps speeds with lightning-fast latency, and premium plans can offer even faster speeds. 

Another factor that separates fiber from satellite is symmetrical speeds, meaning that download and upload speeds are the same. Better upload speeds matter for transferring large amounts of data, video calling, live streaming, and overall bandwidth. Those running home businesses with servers benefit most from symmetrical speeds. Starlink is working toward 1 Gig speeds and better latency, but still lacks symmetrical speeds, with upload speeds that lag behind its top download speed. It's unclear when Starlink can rival these speeds, and as more people in a single area adopt it, congestion will always be a factor.

When does Starlink make sense in the city?

Starlink is the obvious choice for rural homes with few to no high-speed internet options, but it's hard to recommend in a big city or suburban area when there are so many more cost-effective choices. That doesn't mean Starlink doesn't have its place and can actually be a great choice in certain cases.

Even if you're surrounded by choices, they may not be appealing, especially if certain ISPs have burned you for frequent outages, poor customer service, or below-par performance. Fiber is great, but still slow to roll out and may not reach your neighborhood for a long time, if ever. Starlink is one of the few ISPs available anywhere in the U.S. If you're not a fan of your DSL, cable, or 5G options, and you're in a location that's optimal for Starlink, it's a viable option if you're willing to pay the premium.

Plus, having Starlink on hand, even when not active, is handy as a backup internet source. When your main provider goes down, Starlink can get you back online immediately. It even has a very cheap Stand-by mode that gives you minimal connection speed to stay in communication. Not to mention, you can take your Starlink with you on a Roam plan for long road trips and camping excursions.

item.title: Starlink vs. Fiber: Which is Better for Your Home in 2026?
item.content:encoded:
Starlink is one of the fastest-growing satellite internet providers and an increasingly popular option for rural customers. With fast speeds, unlimited data, and lower latency, Elon Musk's SpaceX internet service aims to expand access to reliable internet for rural customers.

Fiber internet, on the other hand, offers breakneck speeds at reasonable prices. Providers continue to expand their markets and offer some of the fastest connections available—up to 8Gbps in some cases.

Determining which internet type is best for you can be challenging. To help you make the best decision possible, we'll examine the pros and cons of both Starlink and fiber services.

In short:

  • Choose Starlink if you live in a rural area without fiber access or need internet for a camper/RV.

  • Choose Fiber if it's available at your address. It offers symmetrical speeds, lower latency (<15ms), and cheaper monthly rates.

item.title: What to Consider When Comparing Satellite Internet Plan Costs
item.content:encoded:
Satellite internet is the ultimate off-the-grid option for staying connected to the web, and it's important to find the right solution that meets your expectations for value, performance, and reliability. 

Like any internet provider, pricing can be tricky, and it's essential to know what you're getting into so you get the best value out of your investment. Several additional charges can make your final bill look very different from the attractive low price that originally piqued your interest. There are also conditions intentionally kept hidden until the last minute that may make the service less worth the price.

Consider these factors when shopping for internet to balance your rural internet needs with the right value.

item.title: Starlink Mobile is on Its Way to Be Major Carrier
item.content:encoded:
SpaceX has officially thrown its hat in the mobile carrier ring, making clear its intention to become a major U.S. carrier with Starlink Mobile. The company celebrated two major developments that bring it closer to its goal of becoming a mobile carrier that competes with the U.S. big three: T-Mobile, Verizon, and AT&T. 

The Federal Communications Commission gave the green light for a 15,000-satellite constellation dedicated to Starlink Mobile, consisting of next-generation satellites with more power to take advantage of recent spectrum acquisitions and communicate directly with mobile phone antennas.

Most recently, SpaceX announced the acquisition of spectrum in the 800 MHz band, clearing the way for broad deployment of a terrestrial network that works alongside satellite coverage. SpaceX has made it clear it will need both to be a carrier with comprehensive coverage. Starlink's satellite coverage makes it available nearly anywhere, eliminating dead zones, but more ground spectrum, including from towers, will be necessary for phones to work in buildings.

The Starlink Standard kit is actually the third iteration of the satellite internet provider's hardware. It replaced the Standard Actuated kit with a more straightforward design that doesn't require the motorized stand. It is larger and more powerful than the Mini, designed to achieve higher speeds in stationary use. The Starlink Mini is ideal for portability and can be used on the go, but it's more expensive and less powerful than the Standard. In this guide, we'll break down all the key differences between the Starlink Standard and the Starlink Mini.

Reselling services on a Residential or Roam plan violates Starlink's Terms of Service. Starlink has been known to suspend service for accounts if it detects higher-than-normal data usage, determines the user may be using it for business purposes, and urges them to switch to a Priority/Enterprise plan to resume service. 

The community site plan may be a compromise for users who don't want a full business plan but want to distribute access to a modest number of people in their community. It's also a way for the company to combat the secondary market for its service, such as owners who rent out their Starlink kits for a profit, another violation of its Terms.  

Depending on the scope of usage you describe in your sign-up form, Starlink may recommend a business plan. The program seems geared toward spaces like community centers, public spaces, rural businesses, single buildings with multiple residences, or multiple households in close proximity. 

An ideal use case could be low-income areas without reliable internet access, where the host's Starlink income contributes to subscription costs and other community needs. It's still hard to tell, since it's unclear what the host's share of the pass revenue will be.
